this a subject that is considered a basic part of many video games, because of how simple it is practice by this point. talking about how its nuts and bolts work exactly is a more extensive topic nobody really goes into, so, i will in this post seeing as I'm currently trying to repair my own grappling hook script.

this will cover some topics that seem basic at first, but add up to a broader picture here.

HITSCAN VS PROJECTILE VS WAYPOINT

hitscan: the game draws an instant laser-accurate line between two points, scanning the space in between, and then doing various things to the line.

99% of all the FPS guns you have shot have been hitscan. there is no bullet drop-off. there is no flight time. these fire to the edge of their length and vanish into thin air. yes, some of them aim inaccurately, but that's only a distance to accuracy stat calculation as run through a random number module. yes, some of them like shotguns have MULTIPLE "bullets" but these are merely redundant lines, or one line with a lot of target detection and randomization being applied.

a grappling hook that hooks in instantly (most of them) use this system.

projectile: the game creates/teleports in a distinct projectile which can be acted on by scripts, or perform its own behaviour via its own script.

these will be missiles, grenades, arrows, bullets with drop-off, etc. if it EXISTS, does a thing, and then ceases to exist or act once it is done doing its thing, you're probably dealing with a projectile. these have drop-off, flight time, they are, you can see them and touch them in-game...or, rather, they touch you mostly. you get the idea.

on a grappling hook, this would be one where you needed to figure out firing it at correct angles so the physics hit the target. an arrow with a cable attached basically.

way-point: specialty marked zones and hooks. the system decides. there is no aiming. you either can, or you cant, and the system directs your shot.

if you've played a game where the hook was a special ability used only on or from certain special objects. that is a waypoint. everything here is mapped. it is IMPOSSIBLE to aim at a point the game does not in the code already. very linear. these mostly appear in puzzles or platforms.

this is used mostly for systems that are highly linear, and often locked off behind special tools/powers/character.

WHERE AND WHAT IS PLAYING SOUND

the following parts might be playing several noises at distinct times. choose these to your design taste

the gun: initial firing noise, misfire, "reeling in"

the hook: hook hit, hook removal

the rope (or to be more exact, the midpoint between hook and gun): "reeling in" (closer to the hook = louder noise), rope friction

SO YOU'VE JUST HOOKED THE HOOK, NOW WHAT?

okay, system decided, you're hooked in. its time to grapple. how does this step work out?

in its most basic form the game now pulls you in the direction of the landed hook (hitscan line render). is that good enough?

NO, we're just getting started. buckle up, now we get more refined.

QUESTIONS REGARDING HOOK CONTROLS

firing key: usually shoot, fires the hook. what happens if you let go of the control after the hook is in? does it cut off or keep itself nailed? how does the hook get broken if it persists? do you hit shoot again or does the unhook command come from a different key

reeling in and out: how does the reeling in work? does it happen automatically? how fast? can you reel and unreel at your leisure?

range of the hook for firing and hanging: if it is a viable object/surface within reach in the level, assume the player WILL use the hook to try and break your game by grappling off of the map. this will happen. account for it.

FIGHTING GRAVITY

oh yes, did you think you were going to escape this one? unless you disabled gravity on the object while grappling or gravity is a moot point, you're dealing with this factor.

the player in motion is a physical object with its own inertia upon which gravity slowly acts throughout reeling you in. UNLESS YOU ACCOUNT FOR IT, GRAVITY WILL SLOWLY DRAG THE PLAYER DOWN, grounding you and preventing you from fully reeling in to higher hook locations. combating this generally requires coding in a mechanism that records the players vertical level, resetting it regularly and thus prevents loss of height during gameplay. whether this means fully reeling in or restricting the player to a rope swing is up to you.

DOES THE CABLE BREAK?

okay, you've accounted for gravity, the hooks reeling in, but oh fuck, you've just fumbled the shot. you're falling now. in a moment you'll be out of the hooks firing range. at this point, you need to decide what happens when the cable reaches that length.

untreated: player falls endlessly, the rope never breaks, and this can stretch across the map, through walls, persists through teleports, anywhere, anything. it does this because the game hasn't been told to cut the cable yet. you will forever be reeled in on this miles-long cable no matter what happens until the grapple is cut short

breaks: fall out of the radius? obstacle in the way? cable snaps

suspension: players height is locked in and shut to the cable and the hook. in practice, this a rope swing or something like hanging off the ceiling.

LEDGES, AND WHAT THE PLAYER IS HEADING TOWARDS

okay, all the previous things have been accounted for, but you're trying to grapple over a ledge or obstacle and you're not getting over it. what do you do?

well, this is a problem that has to do with the players reeling-in coordinates. if its drawing you straight to the hook, that's what its doing. but, thats not good enough you can clearly see though, yes? you want to go over over/onto the ledge, not to the hook. my, my my, this is a problem isnt it.

solution: you're dragging the player to the wrong place

the place you should be dragging the player to if your intention is to grapple onto a ledge is actually SLIGHTLY HIGHER then the hook is. the hook is at height X, you need to be moving towards height X + Y. the gained height accounts for the player, letting you fall right onto the ledge you only hooked the visible edge of. grappling hooks for platformers or sniper characters would be impossible without this rule

MINIMUM RADIUS ENTERED

question, what happens when the hook is fully drawn in and you're there? what happens at that point

untreated: the game in a futile effort to complete its programming, keeps attempting to draw you in closer and closer to the point where objects collide, walls are moved through, and so much jittering happens you might literally cause a player to have a seizure. EXTREMELY UNSIGHTLY AND IMMERSION BREAKING

snap break: cable is simply cut, job being completed

hanging: cable is stopped X distance from completion, thus letting the player endlessly bob and dangle on the place they're stuck to.
